newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran leader vows to defend Jerusalem at summit.
newsitem.headline: Iran leader vows to defend Jerusalem at summit.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on Saturday condemned a U.S. House of Representatives resolution calling on President Bill Clinton to reaffirm that Jerusalem must remain Israel's undivided capital.

He said the U.S. "conspiracy to recognise Holy Qods (Jerusalem) as capital of the illegal state of Israel" would be discussed at a summit of eight Moslem countries set to open in Turkey on Sunday, the Iranian news agency IRNA reported.

"...The impudent move of the U.S. House of Representatives to shift the American embassy to (Jerusalem) indicated Washington's disregard for the world of Islam and Arab states," he told reporters before leaving for Istanbul.
"We should get prepared to defend the sanctities of the world of Islam," IRNA quoted him as saying.

The summit is set to launch the Developing-Eight (D-8) economic cooperation group bringing together Bangladesh, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Turkey to develop trade and industry.
Earlier, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Mahmud Mohammadi said the decision "unmasks the real face of those who claim impartiality in the so-called Middle East peace process".

Tuesday's decision also violated "the spiritual rights of Moslems over Jerusalem and would encourage Israel's expansionist designs", IRNA said in a report monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
Israel, which captured Arab East Jerusalem in 1967 and annexed it in a move unrecognised by the international community including the United States, has welcomed Tuesday's 406-17 vote.

The House vote, which does not oblige the Clinton administration to act, took place as Egypt and other Arab countries struggled to resolve a peacemaking crisis between Israel and the PLO which erupted when Israel began work in March on a 6,500-home Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The Palestinians, who regard East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state, have termed the resolution a declaration of war.
